questions.question: How do event capturing, the target phase, and bubbling work?
questions.title: DOM event propagation phases
questions.direct_answer: A propagating DOM event follows a path through ancestors toward its target during capture, reaches the target, and then travels back through ancestors during bubbling when the event type bubbles. Listener options determine which phase invokes a handler.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the event path and listener phases.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing capture and bubble as two different events or assuming every event bubbles.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Propagation follows the event's composed path; shadow boundaries and non-bubbling events can change what an outer listener observes.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Capture moves from outer ancestors toward the target.
At target, listeners registered for that target can run.
Bubble moves from the target back through ancestors when bubbles is true.
Listeners use the bubble phase by default; `{ capture: true }` selects capture.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- Event propagation lets one dispatched event be observed at several nodes along a path. The capture phase visits ancestors from the outside toward the target, the target phase reaches the dispatch target, and the bubble phase moves back through ancestors if that event type bubbles.

- `addEventListener()` uses the bubble phase by default. Passing `{ capture: true }` registers the listener for the capture side of the path, which can observe the event before descendant bubble listeners run.

- For example, clicking a button inside a card can invoke a document capture listener, then the button listener, then card and document bubble listeners. It is still one click event, and `event.target` remains the button as listeners run on different ancestors.

- Not every event bubbles. `focus` and `mouseenter` are common examples, while `focusin` does bubble and may suit delegation.

- Propagation is useful for coordination and delegation, but handlers should not depend on an undocumented global order. Component boundaries and explicit ownership keep behaviour understandable.

sections.title: One event, one calculated path
sections.content: Before listeners run, the browser determines a path related to the target. Capture and bubble are directions along that path, not separate copies of the event. At-target ordering has precise platform rules, so application code should express required coordination directly rather than relying on accidental listener registration order.

sections.title: What changes at a shadow boundary
sections.content: Events have `bubbles` and `composed` properties. A composed event can cross a shadow boundary, while the target visible to outer code may be retargeted to protect the component's internal structure. `event.composedPath()` exposes the path allowed to the current listener. These rules are why a document listener may not see the exact internal node that originated a component event.

sections.title: A click through nested elements
sections.content:
CAPTURE: window → document → body → card → button
TARGET:                                           button
BUBBLE:  button → card → body → document → window
         (`event.target` stays the original target)

questions.question: What is the difference between preventDefault() and stopPropagation()?
questions.title: preventDefault versus stopPropagation
questions.direct_answer: preventDefault() asks the browser not to perform a cancelable event's default action, while stopPropagation() prevents the event from continuing to other nodes on its propagation path. One does not automatically do the other's job.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to separate browser default actions from event listener propagation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using stopPropagation to stop form submission, or preventDefault to stop an ancestor click handler.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: preventDefault has no effect on a non-cancelable event, and passive listeners cannot cancel their event with it.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: preventDefault() cancels a cancelable browser default action.
stopPropagation() stops later nodes on the event path.
stopImmediatePropagation() also stops later listeners on the same node.
Neither method should be called automatically without a behaviour reason.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `preventDefault()` and `stopPropagation()` control different systems. `preventDefault()` cancels the browser's default action for a cancelable event, while `stopPropagation()` keeps the event from moving farther through its capture or bubble path.

- For example, a form submit handler can call preventDefault to keep the browser from navigating and then perform client-side validation. The submit event can still reach ancestor listeners unless propagation is separately stopped.

- A nested button can call stopPropagation to keep a parent click listener from running, but that does not cancel the button's own default behaviour. `stopImmediatePropagation()` is stronger because it also prevents later listeners on the current node from running.

- Cancellation has boundaries. `event.cancelable` must be true, and a passive listener cannot successfully call preventDefault for the event it observes.

- These methods are escape hatches, not standard boilerplate. Default actions should be canceled only when replacement behaviour exists, and propagation should be stopped only when the component truly owns the event boundary.

sections.title: Default behaviour is separate from listener delivery
sections.content: An event may cause both JavaScript callbacks and a browser action. Clicking a link can notify listeners and navigate; submitting a form can notify listeners and send or navigate. Cancellation addresses the browser action, while propagation addresses which listeners receive the event.

sections.title: Why stopping everything creates hidden coupling
sections.content: An ancestor may legitimately use bubbling for analytics, keyboard support, menus, or event delegation. A descendant that stops every click silently breaks those features. Prefer checking the target and ignoring irrelevant events at the ancestor. Stop propagation only when the nested interaction would otherwise be misinterpreted as the parent's own action.

sections.title: Two independent controls
sections.content:
| Method | Changes | Does not change |
|---|---|---|
| `preventDefault()` | Cancelable default browser action | Propagation path |
| `stopPropagation()` | Delivery to later nodes | Default browser action |
| `stopImmediatePropagation()` | Path plus later listeners on this node | Default browser action |
